3. NonBayesian Hypothesis Testing

3.1. Classification Performance Measures

Problem with Bayesian: priors/costs may be difficult to assign, e.g. medical diagnostic and detecting extraterrestrial life. We will see later from Neyman-Pearson that any good test comes in the form of a LRT:

Theorem 3.1 (Folk5 Theorem). In binary hypothesis testing, for almost any sensible objective, the optimal determinstic rule takes the form of a likelihood ratio test for some 𝜂.

The performance of any decision rule 𝐻̂(⋅) may be specified in terms of the “detection” and “false-alarm” probabilities: In statistics these are the “power” and “size” of the test, respectively.

𝑃𝐷=△ℙ(𝐻̂(𝘺)=𝐻1|𝐻=𝐻1)=TPTP+FN𝑃𝐹=△ℙ(𝐻̂(𝘺)=𝐻1|𝐻=𝐻0)=FPFP+TN (3.1)

3.2. Operating Characteristic of the LRT

A good decision rule contains large 𝑃𝐷 and low 𝑃𝐹, but increasing 𝜂 to increase 𝑃𝐷 comes at the expense of increasing 𝑃𝐹. To see this, consider the operating characteristic curve: plot (𝑃𝐹,𝑃𝐷) while varying 𝜂 from ∞ to 0.

Proposition 3.1. OC-LRT is nondecreasing function.
Proof
Start at (0,0) with 𝜂=∞. Decreasing 𝜂 only increases both 𝑃𝐷 and 𝑃𝐹, so this is trivial.

□

Since it’s an LRT, the Bayesian hypothesis test corresponds to a point on the OC-LRT. How can we find it?

Proposition 3.2. In general, the Bayes risk looks like 𝜑(𝐻̂)=𝛼𝑃𝐹−𝛽𝑃𝐷+𝛾 where 𝛼,𝛽,𝛾>0 are determined by costs and prior probabilities.
Proof

Apply tower law on the cost, this conditioning on 𝘏:

𝔼[𝔼[𝐶(𝘏,𝑓(𝘺))|𝘏]]=∑𝑖,𝑗𝐶𝑖𝑗ℙ(𝐻̂(𝘺)=𝐻𝑖|𝐻=𝐻𝑗)𝑃𝑗 (3.2)

For binary, we have

𝐶00(1−𝑃𝐹)𝑃0+𝐶10𝑃𝐹𝑃0+𝐶11𝑃𝐷𝑃1+𝐶01(1−𝑃𝐷)𝑃1 (3.3)

Implying

𝛼=(𝐶10−𝐶00)𝑃0,𝛽=(𝐶01−𝐶11)𝑃1,𝛾=𝐶00𝑃0+𝐶01𝑃1 (3.4)

□

Proposition 3.2 tells us that the (𝑃𝐹,𝑃𝐷) compatible with the BHT with Bayes risk of 𝑐 yields a line for 𝑃𝐷 and 𝑃𝐹 with fixed slope. Hence we want the smallest value of 𝑐 such that there is an intersection of the Bayes risk line with the OCT LRT:

3.3. Neyman-Pearson Hypothesis Testing

Two popular alternative formulations to BHT is Neyman-Pearson and minimax. We go over the first, in which the objective is:

Definition 3.1 (Neyman-Pearson Objective).

argmax𝐻̂(⋅)𝑃𝐷subject to𝑃𝐹≤𝛼 (3.5)

Note that 𝐻 is not treated as a random variable.

Theorem 3.2 (Neyman-Pearson Lemma, Deterministic Rule). Suppose the likelihood ratio ℒ︀(𝘺) is a purely continuous random variable (i.e. has no point masses) under each hypothesis. Then a solution to Equation 3.5 among 𝐻̂(⋅) that are deterministic mappings is an LRT of the form

𝐻̂(𝑦)=𝐻𝟏ℒ︀(𝑦)≥𝜂 (3.6)
where 𝜂 is chosen such that 𝑃𝐹=ℙ(ℒ︀(𝘺)≥𝜂|𝐻=𝐻0)=𝛼
Proof

Here we sketch an informal greedy proof.

Choosing a deterministic decision rule is equivalent to allocating each element of 𝒴︀ to one of 𝒴︀0 or 𝒴︀1. Consider allocating a neighborhood of volume d𝐲 around a point 𝐲 to 𝒴︀1. Then the contribution to 𝑃𝐹 and 𝑃𝐷 are

d𝑃𝐹=𝑝𝘆|𝘏(𝐲|𝐻0)d𝐲,d𝑃𝐷=𝑝𝘆|𝘏(𝐲|𝐻1)d𝐲=ℒ︀(𝐲)d𝑃𝐹 (3.7)

Now consider a neighborhood of volume 𝑝𝘆|𝘏(𝐲|𝐻0)𝑝𝘆|𝘏(𝐲′|𝐻0)d𝐲 at 𝐲′. Allocating this neighbood to 𝒴︀1 gives

d𝑃𝐹′=d𝑃𝐹,d𝑃𝐷′=ℒ︀(𝐲′)d𝑃𝐹 (3.8)

Hence the approach to maximize 𝑃𝐷 given a fixed 𝑃𝐹 budget is to greedily allocate the neighborhoods with largest ℒ︀(⋅) to 𝒴︀1 first.

The proof is informal in assuming we can sum over neighborhoods with nice densities.

□

3.4. [COOL] Relation to Significance Tests

Recall for any strictly monotone function 𝑔(⋅) we can equivalently implement the LRT as 𝑔(ℒ︀(𝐲)) with threshold 𝑔(𝜂) (inequality flips if 𝑔 is decreasing).

Suppose 𝑃𝐹(𝜂) and 𝑃𝐷(𝜂) are strictly decreasing functions of 𝜂. Then we can let 𝑔(⋅)=𝑃𝐹(⋅), flip the direction of the inequality, and define the p-value as

𝑝∗(𝐲)=△𝑃𝑓(ℒ︀(𝐲))⋛𝐻̂(𝑦)=𝐻1𝐻̂(𝑦)=𝐻0𝑃𝐹(𝜂)=𝛼 (3.9)

where the rightmost equality holds from Neyman-Pearson (Theorem 3.2). This is the probability of observing data with larger likelihood ratio under the null hypothesis.

Tying it to AP Stats: If the likelihood ratio is strictly monotone in another test statistic like the mean, then we can interpret the p-value as the probability of getting a more extreme measurement under the null hypothesis.

3.5. Canis musing on Behrens–Fisher problem

Given two Gaussians with different variances, what’s the optimal test for 𝐻0:𝜇0=𝜇1 and 𝐻1:𝜇0≠𝜇1.

There’s a result that says: For the equal-variance Gaussian two-sample problem, the pooled one-sided t-test is: UMPI: uniformly most powerful invariant (i.e. among tests that are invariance to translating or scaling the units of the data), the t-test is optimal:

If you don’t assume equal variances then Welch’s t-test has weaker status. The sampling distirbution dosen’t work out to something perfectly known like a t-distribution.
